items.question: List<T> versus array versus Dictionary — how do you choose?
items.answer: Array when the length is known and will not change (a decoded SQS batch you will not grow). List<T> when you append. Dictionary when the operation is lookup by key (Redis-style cache, auth tenant map). HashSet when the question is membership. Queue when order is FIFO and you drain from the front. Pre-size Dictionary with expected count to avoid resize GC spikes.
followUps: Why is List<T> not a concurrent structure?
When would you use FrozenDictionary instead?
items.sixtySeconds: Array = fixed. List = grow. Dictionary = key with comparer and capacity hint. HashSet = unique. Queue = FIFO. None replace Channel for multi-producer work or Redis for cross-process.

items.question: What happens internally when a Dictionary grows beyond its load factor?
items.answer: Dictionary doubles its bucket array and rehashes every existing entry into the new buckets. Each resize is a gen-0 allocation plus O(n) rehash work. Without a capacity hint, inserting 100k items triggers roughly log₂(100k) resizes. In production, pass the expected count to the constructor and watch gen-0-gc-count with dotnet-counters during bulk loads.
followUps: What is the default load factor?
How does IEqualityComparer affect bucket placement?
items.sixtySeconds: Load factor ~72%. Exceed it → double buckets, rehash all entries. Pre-size with expected count. Bad comparer or mutable keys break lookups silently.

items.question: Why does Dictionary need IEqualityComparer and when do you supply one?
items.answer: Dictionary places entries using GetHashCode for bucket index and Equals for chain collision resolution. If those disagree, lookups fail. string keys default to EqualityComparer<string>.Default (ordinal). HTTP headers need StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase. Struct keys need a custom comparer because the default struct equality uses reflection. Always pass the same comparer to Dictionary and HashSet.
followUps: What happens if a key's hash code changes after insert?
How does this compare to JavaScript Map equality?
items.sixtySeconds: GetHashCode picks bucket, Equals resolves collisions. Supply comparer for case-insensitive strings and struct keys. Keys must be immutable after insert. JS Map uses SameValueZero; C# is configurable.

items.question: What does foreach actually call?
items.answer: It obtains an enumerator via GetEnumerator (instance or extension), then loops on MoveNext and Current inside a try/finally that calls Dispose. Types need not implement IEnumerable if they have the right pattern. List<T>.Enumerator is a struct — returning IEnumerable<T> from a method may box it. A null collection throws NullReferenceException. await foreach is the IAsyncEnumerable path — module 13.
followUps: What happens if you mutate a List while foreach is running?
Why can foreach use a struct enumerator without boxing?
items.sixtySeconds: foreach is MoveNext/Current/Dispose. Null throws. List mutation invalidates enumerator via version counter. Struct enumerator boxes only when returned as IEnumerable.

items.question: Why can yield return surprise you in a CSV importer?
items.answer: The method returns immediately with an iterator object. The file is not read until foreach. A second foreach opens the file again. Exceptions surface at MoveNext, not at the call. The compiler generates a state machine class on the heap. If you need a snapshot, call ToList once.
followUps: What does yield break do?
Can you mix yield return and return in the same method?
items.sixtySeconds: yield is deferred state machine. Two enumerations, two passes. ToList to materialize. Exceptions at MoveNext, not call site. Do not hold SqlDataReader across both passes.

items.question: Are collection expressions lazy like LINQ?
items.answer: No. Microsoft documents that a collection expression always creates a collection holding every element, even if the target type is IEnumerable<T>. [..File.ReadLines("huge.csv")] loads the entire file into memory. Use them for literals and spreads of already-materialized data, not for infinite or streaming sequences.
followUps: When were they introduced?
Can they initialize Span<T>?
items.sixtySeconds: C# 12. Eager. Can target arrays, List, Span, interfaces. Not a LINQ query. Never spread a deferred IEnumerable over a large file.

items.question: When would you use FrozenDictionary over Dictionary?
items.answer: When data is loaded once at startup and read millions of times — feature flags, route tables, tenant allow-lists. ToFrozenDictionary does extra build-time work (perfect/minimal hashing) for faster TryGetValue. It is read-only: on config reload, build a new frozen snapshot and swap the reference. It is in-process only — not Redis.
followUps: How does FrozenDictionary differ from ImmutableDictionary?
Is ConcurrentDictionary a good substitute for read-only flags?
items.sixtySeconds: Frozen = static lookup table, max read speed, build once. Immutable = versioned snapshots with structural sharing. Neither crosses process boundaries. ConcurrentDictionary is for writes, not read-only flags.

items.question: Your teammate wrote a custom AsyncQueue with lock and Queue<T>. What do you say?
items.answer: Name Channel<T> from System.Threading.Channels. It provides bounded capacity with backpressure, async waiting via ReadAsync/WriteAsync, and SingleReader/SingleWriter optimizations. A hand-rolled lock + Queue lacks backpressure and async integration. If the data must survive process restarts or cross Lambdas, it is SQS — not any in-process collection.
followUps: When is a custom collection justified?
What about ConcurrentQueue for this scenario?
items.sixtySeconds: In-process async pipe → Channel<T>. Durable cross-service → SQS. Custom collection only when you can name an invariant BCL cannot express, like a fixed-capacity circular buffer with overwrite.

items.question: How do C# Dictionary and HashSet compare to JavaScript Map and Set at runtime?
items.answer: JS Map uses SameValueZero equality — objects compared by reference, NaN equals NaN. C# Dictionary uses IEqualityComparer — configurable, required for struct keys. JS object literals coerce all keys to strings; Dictionary keeps int, Guid, and struct keys natively. JS Set is like HashSet but without a custom comparer. Neither JS Map nor Set is thread-safe; C# has ConcurrentDictionary for multi-writer scenarios.
followUps: When would you use a JS object instead of Map?
What about Record<string, T> in TypeScript?
items.sixtySeconds: Map ≈ Dictionary with configurable equality. Set ≈ HashSet. Objects coerce keys to strings — not a real hash map. C# struct keys need IEqualityComparer. Concurrent variants only in C#.

items.question: An API returns IEnumerable<Order> and the caller calls Count() then foreach. What is wrong?
items.answer: If the IEnumerable is deferred — yield, LINQ, or database-backed — Count() enumerates the entire sequence once and foreach does it again. That is two full passes, possibly two database round-trips. Return IReadOnlyList<Order> if the data is materialized, or document that the sequence is single-pass. If the caller needs both count and iteration, materialize once with ToList.
followUps: What return type would you use for a paginated API?
How does this differ from IAsyncEnumerable?
items.sixtySeconds: IEnumerable may be deferred. Count + foreach = two passes. Return IReadOnlyList when materialized. ToList once if caller needs multiple walks. IAsyncEnumerable is async pull — module 13.
